New primary abstracts positively link that Developmental Science report to the earlier in-press Cognitive Psychology work and confirm its7.5/4.5-month design; the shipped Cognitive Psychology report contains eight experiments across7.5–11.5months, beyond the Experiment3copied here. Neither complete original body was recovered after the bounded16-request pair/supplement investigation. Thus the current direct-control comparison is positive, but whether the7.5-month control observations are independent of, or preliminary/alternate reporting of, empirical comparisons already contained in the whole shipped paper cannot be established from the two abstracts and later current account. The4.5-month extension and distinctDOI/pages alone do not certify a separate additional original for this9.5-month test. decisions.quote:
We report a replication experiment of a mechanized version of the seminal wide-screen/narrow-screen design of Wilcox and
           Baillargeon (1998) with 9.5-month-old infants (𝑁 = 80). Two different methodologies were employed simultaneously: (a) the
           standard looking time paradigm and (b) eye tracking.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files (0ab1768ae9c6e310.json, 0ab1768ae9c6e310.state.json) do not yet exist. Both shipped and blind coding agree on type="replication". The paper collects new empirical data from 80 9.5-month-old infants using standard looking-time and eye-tracking methodologies to re-test the wide-screen/narrow-screen experiment of Wilcox and Baillargeon (1998, Cognitive Psychology [4, Exp. 3]).

Pairing was flagged for same_author_year_siblings because the reference list cites two 1998 articles by Wilcox and Baillargeon: Reference [4] in Cognitive Psychology (vol. 37, no. 2, pp. 97-155, DOI 10.1006/cogp.1998.0690) and Reference [5] in Developmental Science (vol. 1, no. 1, pp. 127-142). Both shipped row 168 and blind target_index 0 identify Reference [4] (specifically Experiment 3 with 9.5-month-old infants) as the primary replicated original study.

decisions.quote:
Across conditions with three different screen sizes, the results from both
           methodologies revealed a clear and interesting pattern: the looking times increased as a significantly linear function of reduced
           screen sizes, that is, independently of the number of different objects involved. There was no indication in the data that the infants
           made use of the featural differences between the different-looking objects involved.
decisions.location: abstract, p. 1 (and Section 4.1, pp. 5-6; Section 5 Discussion, pp. 9-10)
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files do not yet exist. Both shipped row 168 and blind target_index 0 code outcome="mixed". In the Discussion (pp. 9-10), the authors state an explicit overall verdict that their results "partly replicate the results from the wide-screen/narrow-screen design originally devised by Wilcox and Baillargeon [4]": infants looked significantly longer in the Narrow-Test condition than in the Wide-Test condition under both SLTP and eye tracking, replicating the main Wide vs. Narrow contrast of [4, Exp. 3], but contrary to [4], looking times increased linearly with reduced screen width rather than showing a qualitative categorical shift and provided no evidence of featural discrimination between the objects.
